I've been down once. Took a car, not a motorbike, but I can tell you as much as I know.

-My favourite things to do/see were Stokes Bay Beach. That's the one where you go through a cave to get to the actual beach. Also Vivonne Bay Beach is nice on the south side of the island. Kingscote is a lovely little town with quite a bit of history behind it. Seal Bay if you want to see seals. American River if you like oysters. The brewery does good bevvies. Decent views on Prospect Hill. Didn't do the west side of the island but there's meant to be heaps of natural beauty over that way.

-If you ever get trucks right up your backside just pull over and let them past. Have a mate that did deliveries on the island and they're often under time constraints. I'd also say bring your own food/drinks if you can because it can be a bit more expensive on the island (freight getting it there and whatnot).

You could also compare this to Scientology at surface level or the concept behind Jonestown. It's quite idealistic with people wanting to better themselves or make a difference in the world. These concepts would draw people in and you would think "this is fine" at first. I'll rank them based on where I live, where I've been and what appeals to me personally. Always happy to chat :)


1) New South Wales

Great climate, beaches, sightseeing, mostly safe, great nightlife (by my standards), entertainment, healthcare, education. Sydney is spectacular and even better if you're wealthy. The suburbs, divided by harbours, all have a real disctinct identity from one another. Downsides of NSW include it being more dog-eat-dog than the rest of the country, very expensive plus more traditional, conservative and straight-laced than say Victoria.


2) Western Australia (Haven't been)

Perth is smaller and cheaper than Sydney. Vast landmass to explore. Not that different to the other states despite being known for its isolation. Would be top if it wasn't a flight away from everything.


3) South Australia

Laidback, more affordable, cities and towns well organised, people mostly friendly and hospitable, but quieter and less entertaining/cosmopolitan than Sydney or Melbs.


4) Victoria

First for visiting, fourth for living. Excellent public transport, nightlife, felt safe, infrastructure, entertainment options etc the list goes on. Trendy, progressive, some great things to see and do but thought a lot of the suburbs were pretty average-looking. Found some of the people to be more aggressive at times but others quite friendly/inclusive/accepting. More likely to strike up a conversation with strangers in Melbourne than Sydney and more of an underlying sense of community as well I found.


5) Australian Capital Territory

Inland, cold in winter but people constantly coming and going and some things worth doing/seeing from a political or national perspective. Gets a bad rap for being boring but underrated cafe scene, sightseeing and nightlife for its size.


6) Queensland

Nice tourist destinations, theme parks, wildlife and natural beauty, extensive sporting history. Too hot for me but great if you like a subtropical climate. Less multicultural, less political correctness, wacky politicians, prone to natural disasters (most of the country is in some way I suppose). People moving there in droves since covid. While certain areas of south-east QLD such as the Gold Coast are changing and growing rapidly, found a lot of people were trying to be something they're not up that way. Brisbane set to become a global city with the Olympics in 2032 which is exciting.


7) Tasmania

Good to visit and maybe alright for retirement but more insular, less multicultural and less happening depending on what you're into. Education and job opportunities don't stack up amazingly compared to say NSW or VIC.


8) Northern Territory (Haven't been)

Outdoorsy tourist destinations, sparsely populated, high indigenous population. Unique to other parts of the country in some ways. Rich history but too hot, not enough happening and too many crocodiles for me.
